A-B-Testing.definition: Showing two random groups of users two versions of something (option A and option B) and measuring which one does better. Online firms can run thousands of these a year because every click and delay is recorded. It lets data, not rank, settle arguments.
A-B-Testing.title: A/B Testing

AI-Agents.definition: An agent is software (the harness) that directs an AI model to do a task, uses ordinary tools to check the result, and retries without a human in the loop. Thompson dates working agents to late 2025 (Claude Code with Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2-Codex). Agents use far more compute than chatbots, and they make the model plus harness pair, not the model alone, the thing that matters.
AI-Agents.title: AI Agents

AI-Compute-Demand.definition: The recurring claim that demand for AI computing power exceeds supply, which is used to justify the huge capex (capital spending on data centers and chips) of the hyperscalers (the largest cloud companies: Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Oracle).
AI-Compute-Demand.title: AI Compute Demand vs Supply

AI-Diffusion.definition: How fast AI actually spreads into real companies and the wider economy, as opposed to how capable the models are. Diffusion is slowed by habit, by trust, and by firms keeping humans in the loop to avoid costly mistakes.
AI-Diffusion.title: AI Diffusion

AI-Stack-Integration.definition: The idea that one company owning every layer of AI (chips, data centers, models, data tools, security, and apps) can build better and cheaper products than companies that own only one layer. Each layer feeds the others: apps show what models need, and chips lower the cost of running the models. Google is the main example. The open question is whether a big, spread-out company can turn that ownership into focus.
AI-Stack-Integration.title: Full-Stack AI Integration

AI-Sycophancy.definition: The habit of chatbots to agree with the user and tell them what they want to hear. Critics say it keeps people hooked, like social media feeds, and can mislead lonely or vulnerable users. Thompson notes it is the opposite of the popular fear that AI will act on its own against us.
AI-Sycophancy.title: AI Sycophancy

Agentic-Commerce.definition: Shopping done or guided by AI agents instead of a person browsing a store or search results. It raises the question of who owns the customer: the store, or the agent that shops on the customer's behalf.
Agentic-Commerce.title: Agentic Commerce

Agentic-Web.definition: The idea that AI agents, not people, will become the main readers of the web. Agents do not look at ads, so the ad and subscription models that paid for web content stop working. That raises the question of how content gets paid for and kept open when the reader is software.
Agentic-Web.title: The Agentic Web

Aggregation-Theory.definition: Ben Thompson's 2015 framework for how the internet reshapes industries. The internet made distribution of digital goods free and transaction costs near zero. So the winners stopped being the firms that owned suppliers, and became the firms that owned the user relationship: the aggregators. They win on user experience, which brings users, which brings suppliers, which improves the experience again (a virtuous cycle). Suppliers get commoditized, meaning they become interchangeable and lose pricing power.
Aggregation-Theory.title: Aggregation Theory

Annualized-Revenue.definition: A guess at a full year's sales, usually one month's revenue multiplied by 12. Fast-growing AI firms quote it because quarterly results look out of date, but it can mislead: one month may not be typical, firms count revenue differently, and the figures often leak through investors rather than formal reports.
Annualized-Revenue.title: Annualized Revenue (ARR)

Answer-vs-Agentic-Inference.definition: Thompson's split between two kinds of AI inference (running a trained model). Answer inference has a human waiting for the result, so speed matters most. Agentic inference is agents doing jobs with no human in the loop, so speed matters less and cheap, large, slower memory matters more. The shift changes which chips and suppliers win.
Answer-vs-Agentic-Inference.title: Answer Inference vs Agentic Inference

Application-Layer-Bridge.definition: Thompson's 2024 idea that each new computing device paradigm is reached through a new application-layer paradigm that first grows up on the old device. Interactive Applications on mainframes bridged to the PC, and the Internet on PCs bridged to the smartphone. He argues generative AI, especially UI generated on demand, is the bridge from the smartphone to wearables.
Application-Layer-Bridge.title: Application Layer Bridge (Computing Paradigms)

Bundling.definition: Selling many products together for one price, like a subscription library. Bundles work when they lower costs or reach more buyers; they fail when the bundled content costs more than the subscriptions bring in.
Bundling.title: Bundling

Capex-vs-Opex.definition: Two budgets a company spends from. Capex (capital spending) is a big up-front payment for something used for years, like a mainframe or a server. Opex (operating spending) is an ongoing payment, like a monthly software subscription. Shifting money inside the capex budget is easier than cutting opex, so a hardware seller can lose a sale fast when buyers want other hardware.
Capex-vs-Opex.title: Capex vs Opex

Capital-as-Ultimate-Commodity.definition: Thompson's 2026 idea that if AI compute stays scarce, getting compute becomes a contest of who can bring the most cash. The advantage compounds, because more compute earns more cash to buy more compute. It flips the old investor preference for asset-light, high-margin tech firms toward capital-heavy businesses that earn bigger absolute profits, the way Berkshire Hathaway used See's Candies cash to buy BNSF Railway.
Capital-as-Ultimate-Commodity.title: Cash the Ultimate Commodity (the Google Capital Company)

Cash-Conversion-Cycle.definition: The number of days between paying suppliers for goods and collecting cash from customers for them. A negative cycle means the firm gets paid by customers before it pays suppliers, so suppliers in effect fund its growth with free short-term loans. Fast-selling inventory and slow supplier payment terms push the cycle down.
Cash-Conversion-Cycle.title: Cash Conversion Cycle

Chain-of-Thought-Monitoring.definition: Watching an AI model's written reasoning trace (its scratch pad of text before answering) to catch bad behavior such as reward hacking or deception. It usually needs a second model to read the trace, so it can roughly double the cost. It works only while models keep reasoning in readable text, which training pressure and new architectures can erode.
Chain-of-Thought-Monitoring.title: Chain-of-Thought Monitoring

Channel-Conflict.definition: When a firm's would-be partners start to see it as a threat, because it sells competing products through other channels or works closely with their rivals. The partners may stop carrying the firm's goods. Gallaugher argues the side that offers the partners more total value usually wins.
Channel-Conflict.title: Channel Conflict

Collaborative-Filtering.definition: Software that spots patterns in what many customers buy or browse and uses them to personalize each customer's experience, such as recommending items that similar shoppers bought. It gets better as more customer data builds up.
Collaborative-Filtering.title: Collaborative Filtering

Commoditize-Your-Complements.definition: A strategy where a firm makes the products that go with its own core business cheap or free, so that demand for its core business grows and no rival can capture the value. Thompson uses it in 2026 to explain why China pushes open weight AI models: free, widely available AI helps China's physical industries like robotics, which are its real strength.
Commoditize-Your-Complements.title: Commoditize Your Complements

Commodity-Cost-Advantage.definition: There are two ways to earn steady profits: be different enough to charge more (the Apple model), or sell a commodity with a lower cost structure than rivals. In a commodity market the price settles where the highest-cost seller earns about zero, so every cheaper seller keeps the gap as profit. Thompson argues AWS runs on this second model.
Commodity-Cost-Advantage.title: Winning a Commodity Market on Cost

Compute-Heat-Rate.definition: A measure tracked by energy analyst Hans Royal: the highest electricity price an AI inference data center could pay and still earn a return. It borrows the power-plant term heat rate, which links fuel input to power output. Because AI inference earns so much per unit of power, the rate is far above normal grid prices, which suggests AI firms can afford to pay much more for electricity.
Compute-Heat-Rate.title: Compute Heat Rate

Conglomerate-Discount.definition: The idea that a company owning many different businesses often trades for less than the sum of its parts would be worth as separate companies. Investors find the mix hard to value and cannot buy only the piece they want. A breakup or spin-off is the usual way to close that gap.
Conglomerate-Discount.title: Conglomerate Discount

Conservation-of-Attractive-Profits.definition: Clay Christensen's idea that profits in a value chain go to the integrated, differentiated part, and leave the modular, commoditized parts. When one part becomes a commodity, profit moves to the next part that can be integrated. Apple is the standard example: hardware integrated with its own software is not a commodity.
Conservation-of-Attractive-Profits.title: Conservation of Attractive Profits

Constitutional-AI.definition: Anthropic's way of training AI models to follow an explicit written set of principles, instead of relying only on people rating answers (reinforcement learning from human feedback, RLHF). Supporters say it makes models safer and more reliable.
Constitutional-AI.title: Constitutional AI

Content-Regulation-Framework.definition: Thompson's 2019 framework for regulating online content. Free speech is guaranteed at the infrastructure level (ISPs cannot block or throttle). General platform providers, like cloud hosts, stay free of liability for what users post and are policed by the market. Only platforms paid mainly by advertising get their own category of regulation, because they earn money from engagement rather than from users paying, so no price signal pushes them to care about harmful content. He also separates what is posted from what the algorithm promotes.
Content-Regulation-Framework.title: A Framework for Regulating Content on the Internet

Contract-Manufacturing.definition: Paying outside factories to make your products instead of owning the plants or employing the workers. It lowers costs and lets a firm grow without building factories, but it adds long lead times and exposes the brand to the contractor's labor, safety, and environmental failures.
Contract-Manufacturing.title: Contract Manufacturing

Cook-Doctrine.definition: Tim Cook's statement of Apple's values, given on the January 2009 earnings call while Steve Jobs was on medical leave. Apple exists to make great products, prefers the simple to the complex, owns and controls the primary technologies behind its products, says no to thousands of projects to focus on a few, and only enters markets where it can make a significant contribution. It became the core of Apple University's teaching on what makes Apple Apple.
Cook-Doctrine.title: The Cook Doctrine

Custom-Silicon.definition: Chips a company designs for its own use instead of buying from Nvidia, Intel, or AMD. Examples: Amazon's Nitro, Graviton (general CPU), and Trainium (AI). The payoff is lower cost per unit of work, not always top speed.
Custom-Silicon.title: Custom Silicon

Data-Asset.definition: Data a firm collects from its own operations and customers (sales by store and hour, clicks, returns) that rivals cannot buy. Used well, it drives better decisions on what to stock, price, and build. Its value comes from being unique and acted on, not from sheer size.
Data-Asset.title: Data as a Competitive Asset

Data-Center-Opposition.definition: Growing local pushback against building data centers, especially for AI. Neighbors worry about power bills, water, noise, and land, and also about AI taking jobs. Because a data center needs local permission to be built, towns and counties can slow or block the AI build-out.
Data-Center-Opposition.title: Local Opposition to Data Centers

De-Minimis-Rule.definition: A U.S. customs rule under which shipments worth $800 or less pay no import duty and skip most customs checks; many other nations have similar rules. Retailers that ship each order straight from a foreign factory to a single consumer, like Shein and Temu, stay under the limit, so their goods arrive cheaper and faster than bulk imports that stores bring in.
De-Minimis-Rule.title: De Minimis Rule (Import Loophole)

Distillation.definition: Training your own AI model on the answers produced by a stronger model, so the student learns to imitate the teacher without the teacher's huge training cost. Chinese labs use outputs from frontier models such as those of OpenAI and Anthropic this way, partly because U.S. chip export controls limit their compute. It is a fast shortcut, but it can leave the copy jagged and hard to tell apart from rivals that use the same teachers.
Distillation.title: Distillation (Training on Another Model's Outputs)

Dollars-Per-Gigawatt.definition: A way to measure how much of a data center's spending one supplier captures, stated as revenue per gigawatt of power the data center uses. Because power is the hard limit on how many AI data centers get built, a supplier grows by selling more of the parts inside each gigawatt (GPUs, CPUs, networking, systems). Nvidia uses it to argue its opportunity per gigawatt rose from about $18 billion with Hopper to $40 billion with Vera Rubin.
Dollars-Per-Gigawatt.title: Dollars Per Gigawatt (Nvidia Revenue per Unit of Data Center Power)

Down-Round.definition: A funding round for a private company at a lower valuation than its previous round. It signals that investors now think the company is worth less than before, though the company still gets new cash.
Down-Round.title: Down-Round

Drop-Shipping.definition: Selling goods the seller never holds. The seller takes the order and passes it to a supplier, who ships straight to the customer. It needs little money to start, but the seller has little control over quality, shipping time, or returns, so customer experience often suffers.
Drop-Shipping.title: Drop Shipping

Dynamic-Pricing.definition: Changing prices on the fly as conditions change, such as raising a price when an item is scarce or when rivals sell out, and cutting it to match a rival. Data and software let an online seller do this constantly. It can lift profit, but shoppers get angry if they feel cheated.
Dynamic-Pricing.title: Dynamic Pricing

Enshittification.definition: Cory Doctorow's word for how maturing tech platforms get worse: once users and suppliers are locked in, the firm changes the service to squeeze more profit from both, for example by filling results with paid ads. Growth goes up while the experience goes down, which opens the door to rivals.
Enshittification.title: Enshittification

Enterprise-Philosophy.definition: Thompson's 2024 idea that enterprise tech is driven by the buyer, not the user: executives who want more revenue and lower costs and judge AI coldly on the bottom line. He compares AI agents to the 1970s mainframe wave, when software replaced clerical workers by executive decision rather than by employees choosing new tools. So the big AI opportunity is top-down company rollouts, not helping workers use chatbots.
Enterprise-Philosophy.title: Enterprise Philosophy (Tech's Third Philosophy)

Export-Controls.definition: US rules that block or limit sales of advanced chips, such as Nvidia's top AI GPUs, and chipmaking tools to China. They aim to slow China's AI progress by starving it of compute. In response, Chinese labs like DeepSeek buy chips on the black market, squeeze more work out of fewer chips, and shift to homegrown chips such as Huawei's Ascend line.
Export-Controls.title: Chip Export Controls

Fast-Fashion.definition: Making clothes in small batches that follow current trends and reach stores in weeks instead of months. Sell what customers are buying now, make less of what they are not, and restock often. Zara built the model; Shein pushed it further online with test batches of a hundred or so pieces.
Fast-Fashion.title: Fast Fashion

First-Best-Customer.definition: Amazon's pattern: build a basic service (a primitive) for its own use, so Amazon is the first and best customer that justifies the cost, then sell the same service to other companies to gain scale. AWS, Amazon's logistics, and the Leo satellite network follow this path.
First-Best-Customer.title: First and Best Customer (Amazon Primitives)

First-Mover-Advantage.definition: The edge a firm can gain by entering a market before rivals. An early lead with a good product can bring big market share, customer lock-in, lessons learned inside the firm, and network effects from partners and skilled workers who build around it. Being first only pays if the firm uses the head start to build assets rivals cannot quickly copy.
First-Mover-Advantage.title: First-Mover Advantage

Flywheel.definition: A loop where each part of a business pushes the next one faster. Amazon's version: lower prices bring more customers, more customers draw more sellers and more selection, more volume lowers costs, and lower costs allow lower prices again. Once it spins, rivals must match every part at once to catch up.
Flywheel.title: Flywheel (Virtuous Cycle)

Gallaughers-Law.definition: John Gallaugher's joke rule: 'Any idiot with funding can ruin a market.' A well-funded entrant that sells below cost, like Pets.com in the dot-com era, can wreck prices for everyone even if its own model can never make money.
Gallaughers-Law.title: Gallaugher's Law

Gamification.definition: Adding game features such as scores, levels, contests, and prizes to work or other non-game tasks to make them less boring and more productive. Amazon warehouses, Uber drivers, and fitness apps all use it. The fun of competing fades fast, so games need to change over time.
Gamification.title: Gamification

Generative-UI.definition: Software screens that an AI builds on request for one person and one task, instead of a fixed app built once for everyone. The interface can be thrown away and made again whenever it is needed. Thompson sees it as the path from today's apps to AI that shows you just the choices you need at the moment.
Generative-UI.title: Generative UI (On-Demand Interfaces)

Hybrid-Cloud.definition: A setup where a firm runs most work on its own computers but uses a public cloud such as AWS or Azure for extra capacity. Shifting load to the cloud during demand spikes is called bursting. It lets a firm avoid buying servers that sit idle most of the year.
Hybrid-Cloud.title: Hybrid Cloud and Bursting

Information-System-Components.definition: An information system is more than technology. It combines hardware, software, data, procedures, and the people who use it. Rollouts fail when firms buy flashy tech without getting the data, processes, and people right, so managers should forecast return on investment and test before launch.
Information-System-Components.title: Information System (Five Components)

Intelligent-Personal-Hub.definition: John Ternus' 2026 name for the device at the center of a person's AI life: always with you, deeply personal, able to run AI models and see and hear the world, and tied to your apps and services. Apple says the iPhone is that hub. Thompson accepts the idea but argues the real hub may be a cloud agent, like Meta's Muse, that runs all the time and may not need apps at all.
Intelligent-Personal-Hub.title: Intelligent Personal Hub

Inventory-Turns.definition: How many times a firm sells through and replaces its average inventory in a period, usually a year. Higher turns mean goods sell faster, cash comes back sooner, and perishable stock is fresher. FreshDirect reported 197 turns a year against about 40 at traditional grocers.
Inventory-Turns.title: Inventory Turns

LATR-Model.definition: Shein's name for its production loop: make a tiny first batch of a new design, show it in ads and the app as a test, and order bigger runs only for items the data says are selling. Because first runs are so small, flops cost little, and thousands of designs can be tested at once.
LATR-Model.title: Large-Scale Automated Test and Reorder (LATR)

LLM-Inflection-Points.definition: Thompson's timeline of AI shifts. One: ChatGPT (November 2022), answers straight from the model. Two: reasoning models, OpenAI o1 (September 2024), where the model thinks before answering and uses many more tokens. Three: working agents, Opus 4.5 (late 2025), where agents call reasoning models many times and one person can run many agents. Each step multiplies demand for compute.
LLM-Inflection-Points.title: Three LLM Inflection Points

License-and-Hire.definition: A deal where a big tech company pays an AI startup to license its technology and hires its founders and key staff, instead of buying the company outright. The startup's investors get paid and a shell company is left behind. Buyers use it to get talent fast and to try to avoid the antitrust review a formal acquisition would trigger, though regulators have probed many of these deals anyway.
License-and-Hire.title: License-and-Hire Deal

Local-Inference.definition: Running an AI model on computers you own instead of paying a cloud provider like Anthropic or OpenAI per request. You pay up front for hardware (mostly GPU memory, called VRAM, which sets how big a model fits), then each use is nearly free and your data never leaves your machine. Open weight models (models whose files anyone can download) make it possible; the trade-off is cost, setup work, and models a step behind the best hosted ones.
Local-Inference.title: Local Inference (Running AI Models on Your Own Hardware)

Long-Tail.definition: The huge number of niche products that each sell a little. A physical store only has shelf room for hits, but an online store with a big warehouse or third-party sellers can carry millions of niche items, and together they add up to a large share of sales.
Long-Tail.title: The Long Tail

Mechanistic-Interpretability.definition: Research that explains how an AI model works by studying its internal numbers (activations and weights), not just what it says or does. It is often described as a brain scan of the model. Tools include probes, difference-in-means vectors and circuit analysis, and uses include cheap monitors for bad behavior and, eventually, controlling what a model learns.
Mechanistic-Interpretability.title: Mechanistic Interpretability

Network-Effects.definition: When a product gets more valuable as more people use it. In a marketplace, more buyers attract more sellers and more sellers attract more buyers (a two-sided or indirect network effect). The biggest network tends to pull further ahead, so these markets often end with one or two winners.
Network-Effects.title: Network Effects

Omnichannel.definition: Running stores, website, and apps as one joined system, so customers can buy online and pick up or return in a store, or find an item online while standing in a shop. The goal is more sales and a smoother experience, and it depends on knowing where every item is.
Omnichannel.title: Omnichannel Retail

Open-Weight-Models.definition: AI models whose trained settings (weights) are published so anyone can download and run them, unlike closed models such as GPT or Claude that are only reached through the maker's service. Chinese labs like DeepSeek, Moonshot and Alibaba's Qwen lead here, and their low prices pressure closed-model makers.
Open-Weight-Models.title: Open-Weight Models

Opportunity-Cost-of-Compute.definition: Thompson's idea that AI compute is scarce, so every chip a company uses for one purpose is a chip it cannot rent to someone else. Firms with a cloud or enterprise business give up paying customers when they spend compute on free consumer products. A firm with no cloud business, like Meta, gives up nothing, so it can focus all its compute on consumers.
Opportunity-Cost-of-Compute.title: Opportunity Cost of Compute

Paperclip-Maximizer.definition: Nick Bostrom's 2003 thought experiment. A well-meaning team makes a mistake in a superintelligent AI's goal, for example telling it to make paperclips, and it pursues that goal so single-mindedly that it turns the earth into paperclip factories. The lesson is to be careful what you ask a powerful AI for, because you might get it.
Paperclip-Maximizer.title: Paperclip Maximizer (Bostrom)

Price-Umbrella.definition: A price umbrella is when the market leader charges more than its costs require, because demand is bigger than supply. Rivals can then price below the leader and look cheap, even if their own costs are not lower. When supply catches up, the umbrella shrinks and prices fall toward cost.
Price-Umbrella.title: Price Umbrella (Price Overhang)

Product-Market-Fit.definition: How well a product meets real demand from the customers it targets. With strong fit, customers want the product and the business can grow into a large, profitable one. Early online grocers like Webvan failed largely because suburban shoppers did not want the service; FreshDirect found fit with car-less, time-strapped New Yorkers.
Product-Market-Fit.title: Product-Market Fit

Referral-vs-Distribution.definition: A way to judge whether AI hurts a consumer business. If AI acts as a referral channel, it sends shoppers on to the business, which keeps the customer relationship, like a better Google Search. If AI acts as a distributor, it sits between the business and the customer and reduces the business to an API call (a back-end service the AI calls). The first is mostly good for incumbents; the second is the real threat.
Referral-vs-Distribution.title: AI as Referral Channel vs Distributor

Reward-Hacking.definition: When an AI (or a person or company) hits the goal it is scored on but in a way that defeats the real point of the goal. The system chases the measurable proxy instead of the purpose behind it. Thompson counts it among the alignment problems he worries about most, and applies it to companies as well as models.
Reward-Hacking.title: Reward Hacking

Scale-Economies.definition: When a firm's cost per unit falls as it gets bigger, because fixed costs (warehouses, software, data centers, ad buys) are spread over more sales and big buyers get better terms. A larger rival can then charge less or earn more than a smaller one, which is hard to copy.
Scale-Economies.title: Scale Economies

Seats-Plus-Consumption.definition: Microsoft's 2026 description of how its software will be sold once AI agents do work. Customers still pay a fixed license per person (a seat), but they also pay a metered fee for how much agent work they use, like a cloud bill. The shift answers a threat: if agents replace workers, a pure per-seat business shrinks, so the vendor must earn money from usage instead.
Seats-Plus-Consumption.title: Seats Plus Consumption (Per-User Plus Usage Pricing)

Shapley-Values.definition: A rule from cooperative game theory for splitting a shared gain among the people who helped make it. Each player gets paid by how much they add on average, across every mix of players with and without them. So a rare, hard-to-replace input earns more than one many others can also supply. Computing it exactly is very costly, so in practice it is estimated.
Shapley-Values.title: Shapley Values

Straddling.definition: Trying to hold two strategic positions at once, such as running both stores and a delivery warehouse, and ending up worse at each than a rival focused on only one. The costs and compromises of serving both models keep the straddler from matching the focused firm's efficiency.
Straddling.title: Straddling

Sustainable-Competitive-Advantage.definition: An edge a rival cannot easily copy. Technology alone rarely is one, since it can be bought. Lasting advantage comes from assets like brand, scale, network effects, switching costs, data, and above all from many parts of a business that fit together and reinforce each other, so a copier must match the whole system.
Sustainable-Competitive-Advantage.title: Sustainable Competitive Advantage

Sustaining-vs-Disruptive-Innovation.definition: Clayton Christensen's split from The Innovator's Dilemma. A sustaining innovation makes existing products better in the ways current customers already value, so incumbents tend to get stronger. A disruptive innovation starts out worse for mainstream customers but is cheaper, simpler, or more convenient for a few new ones, so startups tend to capture the value.
Sustaining-vs-Disruptive-Innovation.title: Sustaining vs Disruptive Innovation

Switching-Costs.definition: What a customer loses in money, time, data, or effort by moving to a rival: a paid membership, a library of bought e-books, stored settings, learned habits. High switching costs keep customers even when a rival is a little cheaper or better.
Switching-Costs.title: Switching Costs

Two-Pizza-Teams.definition: Amazon's rule that any project team should be small enough to be fed by two pizzas. Small teams move fast, avoid groupthink, and let several teams try rival solutions at once. It is a way to keep a big company acting like a startup.
Two-Pizza-Teams.title: Two-Pizza Teams

Two-Sided-Marketplace.definition: A business that connects two groups, such as buyers and third-party sellers, and earns fees on their trades instead of owning the goods. It can grow selection fast without buying stock, but must balance both sides and police bad actors.
Two-Sided-Marketplace.title: Two-Sided Marketplace (Platform)

Unified-Content-Business-Model.definition: Thompson's 2023 idea that the strongest content businesses offer the same content two ways at once: free with ads for most people, and a paid subscription with no ads for those who will pay. YouTube is his main example. Serving both groups from one service lets a company reach the most people and still earn the most per fan.
Unified-Content-Business-Model.title: The Unified Content Business Model

VR-vs-AR.definition: Thompson's split: virtual reality is an immersive experience that pulls you out of your surroundings; augmented reality adds to the world you are already in. He argues the difference is about immersion and input method, not whether your eyes are covered.
VR-vs-AR.title: Virtual vs Augmented Reality

Verification-Advantage.definition: Thompson's idea that AI models improve fastest on tasks where you can check the answer, like code that runs or fails. So a company that owns a clear pass or fail signal, such as whether an ad led to a sale, has an edge in training models. Markets are verification machines: with enough volume, their outcomes tell a model what worked.
Verification-Advantage.title: Verification Advantage (Verifiable Data)

Vertical-Integration.definition: Owning more steps of the chain that makes and delivers a product (design, making, shipping, selling) instead of buying them from other firms. It costs money up front but gives control over speed, quality, and data, and makes the whole system harder for rivals to copy.
Vertical-Integration.title: Vertical Integration

Wholesale-vs-Agency-Pricing.definition: Two ways a store can sell a supplier's goods. Under wholesale pricing the store buys the item and sets any retail price it likes, even below cost. Under agency pricing the supplier sets the retail price and the store takes a fixed cut, often about 30 percent. The e-book fight between Amazon, Apple, and publishers turned on which model applied.
Wholesale-vs-Agency-Pricing.title: Wholesale vs Agency Pricing

World-Models.definition: AI models that learn how the physical world works (how things move, fall, and push on each other) so they can simulate it, not just describe it in words. Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind argues much of this knowledge is hard to put into text, so language models miss it. He sees generating realistic video and interactive worlds as proof of that understanding, and as a path to robots, everyday assistants, and AGI.
World-Models.title: World Models

Zero-Data-Retention.definition: A promise from an AI provider that it will not keep a customer's prompts and outputs after a request is done. For most large companies this is a must before they send sensitive work to a model. Fights over retention are fights over trust and over who gets to see and later use the data.
Zero-Data-Retention.title: Zero Data Retention

0xSero.blurb: Anonymous Poland-based tech consultant and YouTuber who runs four Nvidia GPUs at home.

A&P.blurb: Grocery chain that held 80 percent of US grocery sales in the 1920s and 1930s, then fell.

AI Overviews.blurb: Google's AI-generated summaries at the top of search results.

AI21 Labs.blurb: Tel Aviv AI startup founded in 2017 that makes language models and the Wordtune writing apps.

AWS.blurb: Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing business and the largest cloud provider.

Adept AI Labs.blurb: San Francisco AI startup founded in 2021 that built a browser agent for office tasks.

Adobe.blurb: Maker of creative and document software, including Acrobat and the Firefly AI image generator.

Adyen.blurb: Dutch payments processor competing with Stripe; bought billing startup Orb in 2026.

Ahold Delhaize.blurb: Dutch grocery giant, parent of Stop & Shop and Peapod; bought a majority of FreshDirect (2021) then sold it to Getir.
